title: Topology Starts With Sameness
notes: Open the lecture by naming the central change of viewpoint. Geometry may care about lengths, angles, and the particular drawing, while topology asks what survives bending without tearing or gluing. Use the three inspection words, deformation, invariant, and obstruction, as the through-line for the whole chapter.

title: Chapter Problem And Dependency Map
notes: Frame the chapter as a decision problem: when should two spaces count as the same? The dependency map keeps the sequence honest. Euler characteristic gives the first numerical test, homeomorphism supplies the equivalence relation, surfaces supply the main examples, and invariants become the practical language for separating spaces.

title: Euler Characteristic Ledger
notes: Read the ledger as evidence rather than as a finished theorem. The sphere-like cell structures all return chi equal to two, the torus model returns zero, and the disconnected example returns four. Emphasize that the calculation is simple only because the hypotheses choose the right class of surfaces.

title: Euler Theorem Needs Its Hypotheses
notes: Use this slide to slow down the temptation to memorize V minus E plus F equals two. Connectedness prevents separate pieces from adding their own Euler counts, while the separating-loop condition excludes a tunnel. The point is not that counterexamples are technical; the hypotheses are exactly where topology enters.

title: Proof State: Tree And Dual Tree
notes: Present the proof as a state machine. A primal spanning tree records connectedness, and the complementary dual graph becomes a tree only when loops separate correctly. Thickening those two trees leaves two discs with a common boundary, so the arithmetic proof and the sphere picture are the same argument in two languages.

title: Topological Equivalence As Deformation
notes: Translate the informal rubber picture into the formal homeomorphism habit. A deformation intuition is useful, but the actual claim is the existence of a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. The visual route reminds students that points are tracked one-to-one; no tearing, gluing, or collapsing is allowed.

title: Euler Number As Invariant
notes: State the first invariant theorem in operational language. The counts V, E, and F can change when a polyhedron is subdivided or redrawn, but the alternating total is preserved under topological equivalence. This is the prototype for later invariants: compute from a model, then interpret as belonging to the space.

title: Surfaces: Local Plane, Global Difference
notes: Separate local and global information. Every surface point should have a planar neighborhood, or a half-plane neighborhood when boundary is allowed, yet that local test cannot decide whether the whole surface is a sphere, torus, Mobius strip, or Klein bottle. The classification ledger makes that contrast visible.

title: Surface Gallery
notes: Use the gallery as vocabulary, not as classification proof. Students should recognize which examples are closed, which have boundary, and which are hard to embed faithfully in three-space. The sketches are intentionally schematic so attention stays on construction and invariants rather than on pictorial realism.

title: Abstract Spaces And Neighborhoods
notes: Connect the pictures to the abstract definition. A topology is the neighborhood data needed to define continuity without relying on distance. The inverse-image test for continuity is the hinge: it lets homeomorphism make sense for subsets, quotient constructions, function spaces, and surfaces presented without a preferred embedding.

title: Classification Preview
notes: Present classification as a preview of a later proof and as an organizing theorem for examples. Closed connected surfaces split into orientable handle surfaces and nonorientable crosscap surfaces. The formulas for chi are compact ledger summaries, while orientability records information that chi alone cannot always see.

title: Surgery Ledger: Handles And Crosscaps
notes: Make the surgery operations computational. Adding a handle lowers chi by two and preserves orientability; adding a crosscap lowers chi by one and creates nonorientability. The interactive ledger is not a surface renderer, but it is a reliable invariant dashboard for checking moves through the classification list.

title: Same Chi, Different Surface
notes: Use the torus and Klein bottle to show why one invariant is rarely enough. Both have Euler characteristic zero, so chi alone cannot separate them. Orientability supplies the missing distinction. This prepares students for the larger lesson that topology uses suites of invariants rather than a single universal detector.

title: Invariants Separate Pictures
notes: Turn non-homeomorphism into a reusable proof pattern. If a proposed homeomorphism existed, it would carry the chosen operation and its invariant outcome to the other space. The cutpoint artifact models this with graphs: removing a point can preserve connectedness in one model and destroy it in another.

title: Instructor Checkpoint
notes: Run this as an active checkpoint rather than a summary. Ask students to choose an invariant before making a claim. The target behavior is to stop saying that two drawings look different and instead name the preserved feature, compute or inspect it, and explain how a homeomorphism would have to respect it.

title: Recap: The Invariant Habit
notes: Close by connecting the chapter to the rest of the course. Euler characteristic, orientability, connectedness, cut behavior, and fundamental group previews all serve the same habit: replace visual guesswork with homeomorphism-invariant evidence. The final checks record which claims have already been made computationally inspectable.
